name: C1 — Advanced
description: Operate in Spanish for business, academic, and journalistic contexts. Argue a position, navigate Spain vs Latin American variants, and wield refranes and pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo with confidence.

guide.intro: Business Spanish lives a register above everyday speech. Where you'd say 'Te mando el contrato' to a friend, in a meeting you write 'Le adjunto el contrato para su revisión'. Three habits define the register: the formal 'usted/ustedes' and 'le/les', conditional softeners ('le agradeceríamos', 'sería conveniente'), and noun-heavy phrasing ('llevar a cabo una revisión' over 'revisar').

sections.text: Conditional softeners — agradeceríamos, convendría

Spanish business email leans hard on the conditional to soften requests. 'Le agradeceríamos que…' ('We would be grateful if you…') replaces a blunt imperative. 'Convendría revisar' ('It would be advisable to review') replaces 'tenemos que revisar'. The verb is conditional ('-ría'), and the subordinate clause goes into subjunctive ('que nos enviara').

rows.source: Le agradeceríamos que nos enviara la propuesta antes del viernes.
rows.translation: We would be grateful if you could send us the proposal before Friday.

rows.source: Convendría celebrar una reunión para tratar el asunto.
rows.translation: It would be advisable to hold a meeting to address the matter.

rows.source: Estaríamos encantados de recibir su confirmación.
rows.translation: We would be delighted to receive your confirmation.

sections.text: Formal salutations — estimado, distinguido

Open a business letter with 'Estimado/a' ('Dear') plus title and surname: 'Estimado Sr. García', 'Estimada Dra. Pérez'. For very senior audiences, 'Distinguido/a' bumps the formality further. Plurals: 'Estimados socios', 'Distinguidos accionistas'. Close with 'Reciba un cordial saludo' or the very formal 'Le saluda atentamente'.
Nominalization — llevar a cabo, hacer hincapié

Business Spanish prefers verb + noun collocations over single verbs. 'Llevar a cabo un análisis' ('carry out an analysis') sounds more polished than 'analizar'. 'Hacer hincapié en' ('emphasize') replaces 'subrayar'. 'Poner en marcha' ('launch') replaces 'empezar'. These collocations are fixed — swapping the verb breaks them.

rows.source: Hemos llevado a cabo una revisión exhaustiva del contrato.
rows.translation: We have carried out a thorough review of the contract.

rows.source: Quisiéramos hacer hincapié en los plazos de entrega.
rows.translation: We would like to emphasize the delivery deadlines.

rows.source: Pondremos en marcha el proyecto el próximo trimestre.
rows.translation: We will launch the project next quarter.

sections.text: Mixing registers stings. Once you open with 'Estimados socios', stay formal: keep 'ustedes', swap 'pero' for 'no obstante', and replace 'queremos' with 'desearíamos'.

exercises.answer: We thank you for your attendance
exercises.explanation: 'Les agradecemos' is formal plural 'we thank you'; 'asistencia' = attendance.

exercises.explanation: 'Estimados socios' = 'Dear partners'. 'Colegas' (colleagues) also works in some contexts.

exercises.prompt: Spot the register mismatch — which sentence sounds wrong because casual language slipped in?

Hola chicos, vamos a empezar la reunión
Estimados socios, ya vamos arrancando este rollo
Distinguidos accionistas, bienvenidos a esta sesión
exercises.answer: Estimados socios, ya vamos arrancando este rollo
exercises.explanation: 'Estimados socios' is formal; 'arrancar este rollo' (start this drag) is dismissive slang. The casual second option is internally consistent; the third mixes formal and colloquial registers awkwardly.

exercises.prompt: Match the meeting role to its Spanish title
Allow me, on behalf of the company, to welcome you warmly
exercises.answer: Permítanme , en nombre de la empresa , darles una cordial bienvenida

exercises.prompt: Tap the formal pronoun you hear
exercises.spokenText: ¿Cómo se encuentra usted hoy?
exercises.explanation: 'Usted' + 'se encuentra' (formal 'how do you find yourself') is the most formal register; 'tú estás' is informal.

exercises.prompt: Which transition best opens the agenda after greetings?
options: A continuación, pasaremos al orden del día
Yo hablo primero y ustedes escuchan
exercises.answer: A continuación, pasaremos al orden del día
exercises.explanation: 'A continuación, pasaremos al orden del día' (next, we'll move to the agenda) is the standard transition. The others drop register or sound dictatorial.

exercises.prompt: 'La reunión de hoy ___ tres puntos principales' (covers/includes)
exercises.explanation: 'Incluye' is neutral. 'Abarca' (covers) and 'contempla' (considers) also work in formal register.

exercises.answer: Considero (formal weighted opinion) vs. Creo (lighter belief)
exercises.explanation: 'Considero' carries weight and deliberation, typical of formal speech; 'creo' is everyday belief. C1 register prefers 'considero' in board meetings.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase most diplomatically rejects a proposal?
options: Me temo que esta propuesta nos resulta difícil de aceptar
exercises.answer: Me temo que esta propuesta nos resulta difícil de aceptar
exercises.explanation: 'Me temo que' (I'm afraid that) + 'difícil de aceptar' softens the rejection while staying firm.

exercises.prompt: Regarding the price, we hope you can reconsider
exercises.answer: En cuanto al precio , esperamos que puedan reconsiderarlo

exercises.prompt: What does 'ceder en algunos puntos' suggest?
exercises.explanation: 'Ceder' = yield, give in. Standard negotiation language for partial concessions.

exercises.answer: Estaríamos dispuestos a flexibilizar el volumen, pero el precio unitario debe mantenerse

exercises.answer: Dada la relación a largo plazo , estamos dispuestos a hacer concesiones razonables en las condiciones de pago

guide.intro: Academic Spanish is dense, hedged, and impersonal. Three habits set it apart from everyday speech: passive 'se' constructions to depersonalize ('se considera que', 'cabría señalar que'), conditional verbs for hedging ('podría argumentarse que'), and noun-heavy phrasing where English would use a verb ('llevar a cabo un análisis' rather than 'analizar').

sections.text: Impersonal 'se' — se considera, se desprende

Academic Spanish prefers impersonal constructions over 'yo creo'. 'Se considera que…' ('it is considered that…'), 'Se desprende que…' ('it follows that…'), and 'Cabe señalar que…' ('it is worth noting that…') let you make a claim without putting yourself forward. The construction is always third-person singular with 'se' before the verb.

rows.source: Se considera que este modelo es el más adecuado.
rows.translation: This model is considered to be the most appropriate.

rows.source: De los datos se desprende que la hipótesis es válida.
rows.translation: From the data it follows that the hypothesis is valid.

rows.source: Cabe señalar que el estudio presenta limitaciones.
rows.translation: It is worth noting that the study has limitations.

sections.text: Hedging — podría, cabría, parecería

Spanish academic prose hedges with the conditional ('-ría'). 'Podría argüirse que…' ('it could be argued that…'), 'Cabría destacar que…' ('it would be worth highlighting that…'), and 'Parecería que…' ('it would seem that…') soften any claim. Stack hedges to be more cautious.
Citations and attribution

Spanish academic writing uses 'según + author' (according to), 'siguiendo a + author' (following), and 'de acuerdo con' (in accordance with). For paraphrase: 'Como sostiene García (2020)…' ('As García maintains…'). For direct quote: 'En palabras de…' ('In the words of…').

rows.source: Según García (2020), el fenómeno tiene raíces sociales profundas.
rows.translation: According to García (2020), the phenomenon has deep social roots.

rows.source: Siguiendo a Pérez, podemos distinguir tres categorías.
rows.translation: Following Pérez, we can distinguish three categories.

rows.source: En palabras de la autora, 'el modelo es inadecuado'.
rows.translation: In the words of the author, 'the model is inadequate'.

sections.text: Mixing 'yo creo' into academic prose breaks register instantly. Replace 'yo creo que X' with 'cabría sostener que X' or 'se considera que X'.

lessons.title: Hedging claims
lessons.description: Softening academic statements with conditionals and impersonals

exercises.prompt: Which is the most academic way to introduce a hedged claim?
options: Yo creo que el modelo es bueno
Cabría argumentar que el modelo presenta ventajas
exercises.answer: Cabría argumentar que el modelo presenta ventajas
exercises.explanation: 'Cabría argumentar' (it could be argued) + 'presenta ventajas' (presents advantages) is the academic hedged register.

exercises.prompt: Complete the hedge: 'De los datos se ___ que el efecto es significativo' (it follows)
exercises.explanation: 'Se desprende que' = 'it follows that' — academic conclusion phrase.

exercises.prompt: It would be worth highlighting that the sample is limited
exercises.answer: Cabría destacar que la muestra es limitada

exercises.prompt: Match the academic phrase to its function

pairs.right: It is advisable to clarify that

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriately hedged for an academic abstract?
options: Los resultados parecerían sugerir que existe correlación
Los datos demuestran sin lugar a dudas la correlación
Salieron los números y hay relación
exercises.answer: Los resultados parecerían sugerir que existe correlación
exercises.explanation: 'Parecerían sugerir' double-hedges (would seem + suggest), proper for an abstract. The 'sin lugar a dudas' option is too strong; the others are colloquial.

exercises.prompt: 'No ___ que afirmar que la relación es causal' (one cannot)
exercises.explanation: 'No cabe afirmar' = 'one cannot claim'. 'Cabe / no cabe' is the academic 'fits / does not fit'.

exercises.prompt: It could be argued that the data is insufficient
exercises.answer: Podría argumentarse que los datos son insuficientes

exercises.prompt: Tap the academic-register hedge you hear
exercises.spokenText: Cabría sostener que el modelo es viable
options: Cabría sostener que el modelo es viable
Yo creo que el modelo es viable
Pienso que el modelo está bien
exercises.answer: Cabría sostener que el modelo es viable
exercises.explanation: 'Cabría sostener' is the formal academic hedge; the others are personal opinion phrasing.

exercises.prompt: What does 'sin pretender ser exhaustivos' mean in an academic intro?
exercises.explanation: 'Sin pretender' = 'without claiming/pretending to'. Standard academic disclaimer before a literature review.

exercises.prompt: 'Los resultados ___ apuntar a una posible correlación' (would seem to)
exercises.explanation: 'Parecerían apuntar' = 'would seem to point to' — conditional + infinitive academic hedge.

exercises.prompt: Spot the register mismatch in this academic sentence:
options: Cabría señalar que el estudio presenta ciertas limitaciones
Pues el estudio tiene sus fallos, qué le vamos a hacer
Se desprende que el estudio presenta limitaciones
Conviene precisar que el estudio tiene limitaciones
exercises.answer: Pues el estudio tiene sus fallos, qué le vamos a hacer
exercises.explanation: 'Pues...qué le vamos a hacer' is colloquial. The other three stay in academic register.

exercises.prompt: Match the colloquial phrase to its academic equivalent

lessons.title: Citing sources
lessons.description: Attribution and paraphrase in Spanish academic writing

exercises.prompt: Which phrase introduces an author's view?
options: Según García (2020), la teoría es incompleta
García me dijo que la teoría es mala
Yo y García pensamos lo mismo
exercises.answer: Según García (2020), la teoría es incompleta
exercises.explanation: 'Según + author + (year)' is the standard academic citation framework.

exercises.prompt: '___ Pérez, podemos distinguir tres categorías' (Following)
exercises.explanation: 'Siguiendo a + author' = 'Following + author'. Standard paraphrase opener.

exercises.prompt: As the author maintains, the model is incomplete
exercises.answer: Como sostiene la autora , el modelo es incompleto

exercises.prompt: Match the citation phrase to its function
What does 'a juicio de la autora' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'A juicio de X' = 'in X's judgment / opinion'. Common in academic prose.

exercises.prompt: '___ palabras de García, el modelo es inviable' (In the words of)
exercises.explanation: 'En palabras de X' = 'In the words of X' — direct quote introducer.

exercises.prompt: According to recent research, the result is consistent
exercises.answer: Según investigaciones recientes , el resultado es consistente

exercises.prompt: Which is the most academic way to introduce a counter-citation?
options: En sentido contrario, Pérez (2019) sostiene que…
Aunque Pérez no está de acuerdo
exercises.answer: En sentido contrario, Pérez (2019) sostiene que…
exercises.explanation: 'En sentido contrario' (in the opposite direction) is the academic register for introducing a counter-view.

exercises.prompt: Tap the citation phrase you hear
exercises.spokenText: Tal y como afirma Pérez en su obra de dos mil veinte
options: Tal y como afirma Pérez en su obra de dos mil veinte
Como decía Pérez en su libro
Pérez dijo en dos mil veinte
Según Pérez ya en dos mil veinte
exercises.answer: Tal y como afirma Pérez en su obra de dos mil veinte
exercises.explanation: 'Tal y como afirma + author + en su obra de + year' is the most formal citation phrasing.

exercises.prompt: 'A ___ de la autora, la teoría está incompleta' (in the judgment of)
exercises.explanation: 'A juicio de X' = 'in X's judgment'.

exercises.prompt: Match the casual reporting phrase to its academic equivalent
Which is the correct way to introduce a verbatim quote in Spanish academic writing?
options: En palabras del autor: 'el modelo es inviable'
El autor dijo así: el modelo es inviable
El autor dijo eso, que el modelo no sirve
Como decía el autor, así no funciona
exercises.answer: En palabras del autor: 'el modelo es inviable'
exercises.explanation: 'En palabras de X: "..."' is the academic format for verbatim quotes with quotation marks.

lessons.title: Structuring an argument
lessons.description: Connectors and progression in academic Spanish

exercises.prompt: Match the academic connector to its function
Which connector signals a strong contrast in academic prose?
exercises.explanation: 'Sin embargo' = 'however/nevertheless'. 'Pero' is informal contrast; 'sin embargo' belongs in academic prose.

exercises.prompt: 'Por ___ , conviene matizar el resultado' (consequently)
exercises.explanation: 'Por consiguiente / por tanto / por ende' all mean 'consequently' in formal Spanish.

exercises.prompt: In summary, the results support the central hypothesis
exercises.answer: En síntesis , los resultados respaldan la hipótesis central

exercises.prompt: Which transition introduces a concluding paragraph?
options: En definitiva, los datos respaldan la tesis
Bueno, pues eso que digo, la tesis va bien
Y para terminar, lo que decía
exercises.answer: En definitiva, los datos respaldan la tesis
exercises.explanation: 'En definitiva' is the formal academic concluding connector; the others drop register.

topics.title: Society and public discourse
topics.description: Inequality, the welfare state, and public policy

guide.intro: Spanish public discourse has a vocabulary of its own. 'Brecha salarial', 'estado del bienestar', 'desigualdad social' are everyday tokens in op-eds and parliamentary debate. The register lives between academic prose and journalism — formal but accessible. Master the connectors ('cabe preguntarse si', 'es preciso reconocer') and the noun stock to read El País or La Nación with confidence.

sections.text: Core vocabulary — desigualdad, bienestar, derechos

Spanish public discourse repeats a tight set of nouns: 'desigualdad' (inequality), 'brecha' (gap), 'bienestar' (welfare/wellbeing), 'derechos' (rights), 'cohesión social' (social cohesion). The collocations are fixed: 'brecha salarial' (wage gap), 'brecha digital' (digital divide), 'cohesión territorial' (territorial cohesion). Learn the phrases, not just the words.

rows.source: La brecha salarial entre hombres y mujeres se ha reducido.
rows.translation: The wage gap between men and women has narrowed.

rows.source: El estado del bienestar requiere una financiación sostenible.
rows.translation: The welfare state requires sustainable financing.

rows.source: La cohesión social es uno de los pilares del modelo europeo.
rows.translation: Social cohesion is one of the pillars of the European model.

sections.text: Policy verbs — fomentar, impulsar, abordar

Public-policy Spanish uses a specific verb set. 'Fomentar' (foster), 'impulsar' (drive forward), 'abordar' (tackle), 'paliar' (alleviate), 'erradicar' (eradicate). These verbs almost always take noun-phrase objects: 'fomentar la igualdad', 'abordar la pobreza', 'paliar los efectos'.
Rhetorical questions — cabe preguntarse

Op-eds love the rhetorical question. 'Cabe preguntarse si…' ('one might ask whether…'), '¿Hasta qué punto…?' ('to what extent…'), '¿No sería preferible…?' ('would it not be preferable…') frame an argument by inviting the reader to consider an alternative.

rows.source: Cabe preguntarse si las políticas actuales bastan para revertir la tendencia.
rows.translation: One might ask whether current policies are enough to reverse the trend.

rows.source: ¿Hasta qué punto el modelo es sostenible?
rows.translation: To what extent is the model sustainable?

rows.source: ¿No sería preferible invertir en prevención?
rows.translation: Would it not be preferable to invest in prevention?

sections.text: Public-discourse Spanish leans on nouns. Where English says 'we must protect workers', Spanish says 'es preciso garantizar la protección de los trabajadores'. The shift to nouns + 'es preciso/necesario' instantly raises the register.

guide.intro: Spanish refranes (proverbs) and modismos (idioms) carry centuries of folk wisdom and emotional color. They almost never translate literally: 'costar un ojo de la cara' means 'to cost an arm and a leg', not 'to cost an eye of the face'. C1 mastery means recognizing these in conversation, choosing the right register, and avoiding word-for-word translation traps from English.

sections.text: Body-part idioms — un ojo de la cara, no pegar ojo

Spanish idiom-builds heavily off the body. 'Costar un ojo de la cara' (to cost an arm and a leg), 'no pegar ojo' (not sleep a wink), 'estar hasta las narices' (be fed up), 'meter la pata' (put your foot in it), 'tomar el pelo a alguien' (pull someone's leg). The verb is fixed — you can't swap 'costar' for 'valer' here.

rows.source: Ese coche cuesta un ojo de la cara.
rows.translation: That car costs an arm and a leg.

rows.source: Anoche no pegué ojo por el ruido.
rows.translation: Last night I didn't sleep a wink because of the noise.

rows.source: Estoy hasta las narices de esperar.
rows.translation: I'm fed up with waiting.

rows.source: Metí la pata en la reunión.
rows.translation: I put my foot in it at the meeting.

sections.text: Animal idioms — gato, cabra, perro

Animals carry attitudes in Spanish idiom. 'Estar como una cabra' (be crazy, lit. 'be like a goat'), 'dar gato por liebre' (to swindle, lit. 'give cat for hare'), 'ser un lince' (be sharp, lit. 'be a lynx'), 'a otro perro con ese hueso' (tell that to someone else, lit. 'to another dog with that bone'). Native speakers reach for these constantly.
Action idioms — tirar la toalla, ponerse las pilas

Highly productive in everyday speech: 'tirar la toalla' (throw in the towel — give up), 'ponerse las pilas' (put your batteries in — get your act together), 'echar una mano' (lend a hand), 'hacer la vista gorda' (look the other way), 'estar en las nubes' (have your head in the clouds). These are register-neutral — you can use them with your boss or a friend.

rows.source: Después de tantos intentos, decidió tirar la toalla.
rows.translation: After so many attempts, he decided to throw in the towel.

rows.source: Si quieres aprobar, tienes que ponerte las pilas.
rows.translation: If you want to pass, you need to get your act together.

rows.source: ¿Me echas una mano con la mudanza?
rows.translation: Can you lend me a hand with the move?

sections.text: Two traps for English speakers: (1) Don't translate the English idiom directly — 'it's raining cats and dogs' is 'llueve a cántaros' in Spanish, not 'llueve gatos y perros'. (2) Watch for register: 'estar como una cabra' is fine with friends but odd in a formal report. Match the idiom to the situation.

topics.title: Advanced grammar
topics.description: Pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo, cleft 'lo que', advanced relatives

guide.intro: Four high-leverage C1 structures separate intermediate from advanced Spanish: the pluscuamperfecto del subjuntivo ('hubiera/hubiese' + participle) for past unreal conditions; cleft 'lo que' constructions for emphasis; advanced relative pronouns ('cuyo', 'el cual'); and stylistic inversion. Each construction signals literary or formal register and is essential for writing op-eds, essays, and well-spoken arguments.

sections.text: Pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo — hubiera / hubiese

For past unreal conditions ('if I had known…'), Spanish uses 'si + hubiera/hubiese + participle' in the if-clause, and 'habría + participle' (or 'hubiera + participle') in the main clause. 'Hubiera' and 'hubiese' are interchangeable; 'hubiera' is more common in Latin America, 'hubiese' in Spain — but both are correct everywhere.

rows.source: Si hubiera sabido la verdad, no habría venido.
rows.translation: If I had known the truth, I wouldn't have come.

rows.source: Si hubieses estudiado más, habrías aprobado.
rows.translation: If you had studied more, you would have passed.

rows.source: De haberlo sabido antes, hubiera reaccionado distinto.
rows.translation: Had I known earlier, I would have reacted differently.

sections.text: Cleft 'lo que' — emphasis structures

Cleft 'lo que' moves a constituent to the front for emphasis. 'Lo que pasa es que…' ('the thing is…'), 'Lo que más me gusta es…' ('what I like most is…'), 'Lo que necesitamos es tiempo' ('what we need is time'). The structure: 'lo que' + clause + 'es/son' + emphasized item.

rows.source: Lo que pasa es que no tenemos tiempo.
rows.translation: The thing is, we don't have time.

rows.source: Lo que más me sorprendió fue su reacción.
rows.translation: What surprised me most was his reaction.

rows.source: Lo que necesitamos es una solución integral.
rows.translation: What we need is a comprehensive solution.

sections.text: Advanced relatives — cuyo, el cual

Two relative pronouns belong only to C1+. 'Cuyo/a/os/as' = whose; it agrees with the noun that follows, not the antecedent: 'la mujer cuyos hijos…' ('the woman whose children…'). 'El cual / la cual / los cuales / las cuales' replaces 'que' in formal writing after prepositions, especially long ones: 'el problema sobre el cual hablamos' ('the problem about which we spoke').

rows: El motivo por el cual vine
Los temas sobre los cuales debatimos
El director, quien firmó el contrato

sections.text: Common trap: 'cuyo' agrees with the noun it modifies, not its antecedent. 'La empresa cuyos empleados' (the company whose employees) — 'cuyos' is masculine plural because it agrees with 'empleados', not feminine 'empresa'.

lessons.title: Pluscuamperfecto subjuntivo
lessons.description: Hubiera / hubiese for past unreal conditions

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'Si ___ sabido, no habría venido' (If I had known)
exercises.explanation: Past unreal condition: 'si + hubiera + participle' in the if-clause; 'habría + participle' in the main.

exercises.prompt: 'Si hubieses estudiado más, ___ aprobado' (you would have passed)
exercises.explanation: Main clause of past unreal: 'habrías + participle' (conditional perfect).

exercises.prompt: If I had had more time, I would have done it differently
exercises.answer: Si hubiera tenido más tiempo , lo habría hecho de otra manera

Si me decías, te habría ayudado
exercises.answer: Si me hubieras dicho, te habría ayudado
exercises.explanation: Past unreal: 'hubieras dicho' + 'habría ayudado'. The others mix tenses or persons.

exercises.prompt: 'De ___ sabido antes, hubiera reaccionado distinto' (have)
exercises.explanation: 'De + infinitive' is a literary alternative to 'si + hubiera + participle'. 'De haberlo sabido' = 'had I known it'.

I wish you had told me before

exercises.explanation: In past unreal, the main clause accepts both 'habría + participle' and 'hubiera + participle' interchangeably.

exercises.prompt: 'Si lo ___ así, te habría avisado' (had seen — hubiese form)

exercises.prompt: What does 'cuyo' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Cuyo/a/os/as' = whose. Always agrees with the noun that FOLLOWS it, not with the antecedent.

exercises.prompt: 'La empresa ___ empleados protestaron' (whose — masc. pl. employees)

lessons.title: Inversion and emphasis
lessons.description: Stylistic inversion and special structures

exercises.prompt: What does 'Tal es la situación que…' achieve?
options: Strong consequence — 'Such is the situation that…'
exercises.answer: Strong consequence — 'Such is the situation that…'
exercises.explanation: 'Tal es X que Y' — emphatic consequence structure: 'Such is X that Y follows'.

exercises.prompt: 'No bien ___ entrado, sonó el teléfono' (had — no sooner had)
exercises.explanation: 'No bien había + participle' = 'no sooner had' — literary inversion.

exercises.prompt: Such is the importance of the issue that the parliament has met urgently
exercises.answer: Tal es la importancia del asunto que el parlamento se ha reunido con urgencia

exercises.prompt: Match the inversion phrase to its function

Por más que intentar, no lo logro

exercises.answer: Por más que lo intente, no lo logro

exercises.prompt: 'Apenas ___ llegado cuando empezó la lluvia' (had — hardly had)

topics.title: Formal debate
topics.description: Disagree, refute, and rebut in Spanish

guide.intro: Formal debate Spanish is a high-stakes art. The trick: maintain courtesy ('con el debido respeto', 'permítame discrepar') while attacking the argument. Native speakers stack hedges, concessions, and pivots. Never a flat 'no estoy de acuerdo' — instead 'comprendo el planteamiento pero sostendría que…' Master five moves: polite disagreement, conceding then pivoting, refuting evidence, rhetorical questions, and the assertive closer.

sections.text: Polite disagreement

Spanish never disagrees flatly in formal debate. The fixed openers: 'Permítame discrepar' ('Allow me to disagree'), 'Con el debido respeto' ('With due respect'), 'Sin ánimo de polemizar' ('Without wishing to polemicize'), 'Si me permite la observación' ('If I may observe'). Each is a polite shield around the disagreement that follows.

rows.source: Permítame discrepar en este punto, señor presidente.
rows.translation: Allow me to disagree on this point, Mr. Chair.

rows.source: Con todo el respeto que merece su análisis, sostendría lo contrario.
rows.translation: With all the respect your analysis deserves, I would maintain the opposite.

rows.source: Sin ánimo de polemizar, debo señalar una imprecisión.
rows.translation: Without wishing to polemicize, I must point out an inaccuracy.

sections.text: Concede then pivot — si bien… no obstante

The debate move: acknowledge what the opponent got right, then turn. 'Si bien X, no obstante Y' = 'while X, nevertheless Y'. 'Es cierto que X, pero conviene matizar que Y' ('it is true X, but we should clarify Y'). The concession lowers the opponent's guard; the pivot lands the punch.
Refuting evidence

Direct attack on data uses formal verbs: 'Cuestionar' (question), 'rebatir' (refute), 'desmentir' (deny / disprove). 'Los datos que cita no resisten un análisis riguroso' ('the data you cite do not withstand rigorous analysis'). 'Conviene precisar que el estudio adolece de un sesgo metodológico' ('we should clarify that the study suffers from methodological bias').

rows.translation: I question the validity of the sample used.

rows.translation: The data you cite do not withstand rigorous analysis.

rows.source: Permítame rebatir ese argumento con tres consideraciones.

sections.text: Refrán power-move: drop a proverb into a debate and you land twice. 'Como bien dice el refrán, no todo lo que reluce es oro' ('as the saying goes, not all that glitters is gold'). Native debaters use this constantly — it sounds wise without sounding personal.

topics.title: Regional variation
topics.description: Spain vs Latin America — vocab, pronouns, and voseo

guide.intro: Spanish is a federation, not a single dialect. The biggest splits: vocabulary (coche vs carro, ordenador vs computadora), formal-plural pronouns (vosotros in Spain vs ustedes in LatAm), and the voseo (vos in Argentina/Uruguay vs tú elsewhere). At C1 you don't need to switch dialects — you need to RECOGNIZE them. A Madrileño understanding a Porteño without freezing is the C1 milestone.

sections.text: Vocabulary differences

Cars, computers, phones, fruit — everyday objects have totally different names across the Spanish-speaking world. Spain says 'coche', most of Latin America says 'carro'. Spain says 'ordenador', LatAm says 'computadora'. Spain says 'móvil', LatAm says 'celular'. None are wrong; choose by audience. Argentina and Uruguay add another layer with their own vocabulary.

rows: juice (reversed: zumo in Spain, jugo in LatAm)

sections.text: Vosotros vs ustedes

Spain uses 'vosotros' for the informal plural ('you all') with its own conjugation: 'vosotros habláis', 'vosotros tenéis'. Latin America has lost 'vosotros' entirely — both formal and informal plural collapse into 'ustedes' ('ustedes hablan', 'ustedes tienen'). Reading Spain authors? Expect 'vosotros'. Reading Borges? Always 'ustedes'.

rows.source: (Spain) Vosotros, ¿qué pensáis del asunto?
rows.translation: (Spain) You all, what do you think of the matter?

rows.source: (LatAm) Ustedes, ¿qué piensan del asunto?
rows.translation: (LatAm) You all, what do you think of the matter? (Same idea, different verb form)

rows.source: (Spain) ¿Habéis terminado? — (LatAm) ¿Han terminado?
rows.translation: Have you (all) finished?

sections.text: Voseo — vos in Argentina

Argentina, Uruguay, parts of Central America (Costa Rica, Nicaragua, El Salvador) use 'vos' instead of 'tú' for informal singular. The conjugation drops the diphthong and shifts the stress: 'tú hablas' → 'vos hablás', 'tú comes' → 'vos comés', 'tú vives' → 'vos vivís'. Imperative: 'habla tú' → 'hablá vos' (no -d-, stress on final syllable). Pronoun forms 'te', 'tu', 'tuyo' stay the same as with tú.

Don't switch dialect mid-conversation. If you start with 'vosotros' (Spain), stay there. If you switch from 'vosotros' to 'ustedes' to 'vos' in one paragraph, you sound confused. Pick a region and commit — or use 'usted/ustedes' as the neutral universal.

guide.intro: Spanish journalism has its own register — denser than spoken Spanish, looser than academic writing. Three habits define it: heavy attribution ('fuentes próximas a', 'según trascendió'), passive 'se' or third-person plural to convey responsibility without naming, and a noun-rich opening that packs the who/what/when/where into the first sentence.

sections.text: Attribution — fuentes, según trascendió

Spanish news cites with style. 'Según fuentes oficiales' ('according to official sources'), 'fuentes próximas a la investigación' ('sources close to the investigation'), 'según trascendió' ('as transpired / as reported'). These templates let journalists report without naming a single source — a key device for sensitive stories.

rows.source: Según fuentes próximas al gobierno, la decisión es inminente.
rows.translation: According to sources close to the government, the decision is imminent.

rows.source: Según trascendió, el ministro presentará su dimisión mañana.
rows.translation: As transpired, the minister will tender his resignation tomorrow.

rows.source: Fuentes oficiales confirmaron la noticia anoche.
rows.translation: Official sources confirmed the news last night.

sections.text: Lead structure — who, what, when, where

The opening sentence of a Spanish news article packs in maximum info: time, actor, action, place. 'El presidente Sánchez anunció ayer en La Moncloa…' ('President Sánchez announced yesterday at La Moncloa…'). Word order is flexible; the time often comes after the verb.

rows: El gobierno / el presidente / la empresa

sections.text: Op-ed register — cabe preguntarse

Opinion columns reach for rhetorical questions, contrast, and irony. 'Cabe preguntarse si X' ('one might ask whether X'), 'No deja de sorprender que Y' ('it is striking that Y'), 'Resulta paradójico que Z' ('it is paradoxical that Z'). These framings carry the writer's voice without flat first-person claims.

rows.source: Cabe preguntarse si la reforma resolverá el problema de fondo.
rows.translation: One might ask whether the reform will resolve the underlying problem.

rows.source: No deja de sorprender que el ministro mantenga su postura.
rows.translation: It is striking that the minister maintains his position.

rows.source: Resulta paradójico que se invierta tanto y se obtenga tan poco.
rows.translation: It is paradoxical that so much is invested and so little is obtained.

sections.text: Spanish news headlines often drop articles to save space: 'Gobierno aprueba ley' instead of 'El gobierno aprueba una ley'. In the body, articles return. Train your eye for headline-style brevity.

topics.title: Tú, vos, usted — pronoun systems by country
topics.description: Tuteo, voseo, ustedeo, and vosotros — when each is heard

guide.intro: Spanish has three competing second-person systems, and they sort by country, not by formality. Tuteo (tú) rules Spain, Mexico, and most of Central America. Voseo (vos) is the everyday pronoun in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and pockets of Central America (Costa Rica, Nicaragua, El Salvador). Ustedeo — using 'usted' even with parents, partners, and best friends — is the Colombian and Costa Rican norm, and what a Spaniard would mistake for stiff formality. On top of all that, the plural splits: Spain keeps 'vosotros' for informal plural, while Latin America has collapsed everything into 'ustedes'. At C1 you don't need to PRODUCE every system — but you need to RECOGNIZE the speaker's country from a single sentence.

sections.text: Tuteo — tú (Spain, Mexico, much of Central America)

The default global Spanish pronoun. 'Tú hablas', 'tú comes', 'tú vives'. Imperative: 'habla', 'come', 'vive'. Reflexive: 'te'. Possessive: 'tu / tuyo'. Used informally with friends, family, peers, and increasingly even with strangers in Spain. Mexico keeps 'usted' for elders and formal contexts but 'tú' with friends.
Voseo — vos (Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, parts of Central America)

'Vos' replaces 'tú' as the informal singular. The present indicative drops the diphthong and shifts stress to the final syllable: 'vos hablás', 'vos comés', 'vos vivís'. The imperative drops the final '-d' you'd see in a Spain-style 'hablad' and stresses the last syllable: 'hablá', 'comé', 'viví'. The verb 'ser' is wildly irregular: 'vos sos'. Object and possessive forms stay 'te', 'tu', 'tuyo' — only the subject pronoun and indicative/imperative conjugation change.
Ustedeo — usted even with intimates (Colombia, Costa Rica)

In Bogotá and across the Colombian interior, and throughout Costa Rica, parents call their children 'usted', spouses call each other 'usted', and best friends use 'usted'. This is NOT formality — it's the neutral register. A Bogotano saying 'mi amor, ¿usted ya cenó?' to his wife is being affectionate, not distant. A Spaniard hearing this would assume stiffness; that's a misread.

rows.source: (Colombia, husband to wife) Mi amor, ¿usted quiere que le sirva más café?

rows.source: (Costa Rica, mother to toddler) Mi niña, venga, déme la mano.

rows.source: (Spain, same context) Cariño, ¿quieres más café?

sections.text: Vosotros vs ustedes — the plural split

Spain alone preserves 'vosotros' (informal plural) with its own conjugation: 'vosotros habláis', 'vosotros tenéis', 'vosotros sois'. Imperative: 'hablad', 'comed', 'venid'. Everywhere in Latin America 'vosotros' is dead — both formal and informal plural collapse into 'ustedes' with third-person plural conjugation ('ustedes hablan', 'ustedes tienen'). Reading a Spanish novelist? Expect 'vosotros'. Reading García Márquez or Borges? Always 'ustedes'.

If you're unsure which country you're talking to, 'usted/ustedes' works everywhere. It might sound a touch stiff in Spain or Argentina, but no one will misunderstand you. Mixing 'vosotros' into a chat with an Argentine, or 'vos sos' with a Madrileño, immediately marks you as a learner who hasn't picked a dialect.

topics.title: Leísmo, laísmo, loísmo — pronoun variation
topics.description: How direct- and indirect-object pronouns shift by region

guide.intro: The standard Spanish pronoun system splits cleanly: direct objects 'lo/la/los/las', indirect objects 'le/les'. But that clean split is constantly under regional pressure. Central and Northern Spain swap 'le' in for masculine human direct objects (leísmo). Madrid and parts of central Spain swap 'la' in for feminine indirect objects (laísmo). A rare and stigmatized 'loísmo' swaps 'lo' in for masculine indirect. The RAE accepts leísmo for human masculine direct objects only; laísmo and loísmo are non-standard. At C1, you don't need to PRODUCE these variants — you need to PARSE them when you read Cervantes, Pérez-Reverte, or a Madrid newspaper, and convert them back to the standard form in your own writing.

sections.text: Standard system — lo/la for DO, le/les for IO

Across Latin America and in prescriptively-trained American Spanish, the system is regular. Direct object 'I saw him' = 'Lo vi'. 'I saw her' = 'La vi'. Indirect object 'I told him the truth' = 'Le dije la verdad'. 'I told her the truth' = also 'Le dije la verdad' — 'le' is gender-neutral. Plural: 'los/las' for direct, 'les' for indirect. Test: replace the noun phrase with the pronoun and check the verb's transitivity.

rows.source: Vi a Juan. → Lo vi.
rows.translation: I saw Juan. → I saw him. (DO masc.)

rows.source: Vi a María. → La vi.
rows.translation: I saw María. → I saw her. (DO fem.)

rows.source: Le di el libro a Juan. → Le di el libro.
rows.translation: I gave the book to Juan. → I gave him the book. (IO masc.)

rows.source: Le di el libro a María. → Le di el libro.
rows.translation: I gave the book to María. → I gave her the book. (IO fem.)

sections.text: Leísmo — 'le' as masculine human direct object

Central and northern Spain (especially Madrid, Castilla) systematically uses 'le' instead of 'lo' when the direct object is a male person. 'Le vi a Juan' instead of 'Lo vi a Juan'. The RAE accepts THIS variant — but only for masculine human direct objects. Leísmo for objects ('Le tengo' for 'I have it' referring to a book) is non-standard. Plural 'les vi a los chicos' is widely used in Spain but less universally accepted.

rows: Feminine DO: leísmo doesn't touch it

sections.text: Laísmo — 'la' as feminine indirect object

Madrid and surrounding central Spain use 'la' for feminine indirect objects: 'La dije la verdad a María' instead of 'Le dije la verdad'. The system 'fixes' the gender-neutral 'le' by marking it feminine. RAE rejects this — it's non-standard, stigmatized in writing, but extremely common in casual Madrid speech. You'll meet it constantly in dialogue in Madrid-set novels and films.

rows.source: (standard) Le dije la verdad a María.
rows.translation: I told María the truth.

rows.source: (laísmo, Madrid) La dije la verdad a María.
rows.translation: Same — but with 'la' marked as feminine IO. Non-standard.

rows.source: (standard) Les compré flores a las chicas.
rows.translation: I bought the girls flowers.

rows.source: (laísmo) Las compré flores a las chicas.
rows.translation: Same — laísmo plural.

sections.text: Loísmo — 'lo' as masculine indirect (rare, stigmatized)

The mirror of laísmo: 'lo' replaces 'le' for masculine indirect objects. 'Lo dije la verdad a Juan'. This is heavily stigmatized — you'll rarely see it in writing and most Spaniards will laugh at it. Worth RECOGNIZING (some rural speech still has it) but NEVER produce.

If you're writing in Spanish — papers, business email, news — stick to the standard system. Leísmo de persona ('le vi a Juan') is the only acceptable variant in formal writing, and only because RAE specifically blessed it. Laísmo and loísmo will mark your prose as either Madrid-dialect or non-native depending on context.

Le vi a Juan en la fiesta y lo di tu mensaje.
La vi a Juan en la fiesta y le di tu mensaje.
exercises.answer: Lo vi a Juan en la fiesta y le di tu mensaje.
exercises.explanation: 'Ver a Juan' = DO masc. → 'lo vi'. 'Dar tu mensaje a Juan' = IO → 'le di'. The other options are leísmo, loísmo, and ungrammatical respectively.

exercises.prompt: Standard — fill: 'Mis padres ___ regalaron un coche cuando me gradué' (IO pronoun for first person singular).
exercises.explanation: First and second person IO pronouns are 'me, te, nos, os' — they don't have leísmo issues. The variation is only third person.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses standard pronouns correctly?
options: Los llamé y les conté todo.
Les llamé y los conté todo.
Las llamé y los conté todo.
Los llamé y los conté todo.
exercises.answer: Los llamé y les conté todo.
exercises.explanation: 'Llamar a ellos' = DO masc. plural → 'los llamé'. 'Contar todo a ellos' = IO → 'les conté'.

lessons.title: Leísmo de persona — Spain's accepted variant
lessons.description: 'Le vi a Juan' — RAE-accepted for masculine human DO

exercises.prompt: Which is the leísmo de persona variant?
exercises.explanation: Leísmo de persona swaps 'le' in for masculine human direct object. RAE-accepted variant — common in central and northern Spain.

exercises.prompt: Leísmo de persona is accepted for:
exercises.explanation: RAE accepts 'le' for masculine HUMAN DO. Not for things ('le tengo' for 'I have it' is non-standard). Not for feminine ('le vi a María' is non-standard).

exercises.prompt: Convert standard 'Lo conozco hace años (a Pedro)' to leísmo: '___ conozco hace años' (one word).
exercises.explanation: Leísmo de persona: 'le conozco a Pedro' instead of 'lo conozco'.

exercises.prompt: A Madrid newspaper writes: 'El presidente fue detenido y le interrogaron durante horas.' What is 'le'?
options: leísmo de persona — DO that should be 'lo' in LatAm
exercises.answer: leísmo de persona — DO that should be 'lo' in LatAm
exercises.explanation: 'Interrogar' takes DO. Standard: 'lo interrogaron'. Madrid press writes 'le interrogaron' — accepted leísmo.

exercises.prompt: Convert leísmo to standard
exercises.explanation: Each leísmo 'le/les' becomes standard 'lo/los' for masculine human DO.

exercises.prompt: Pick the leísmo version
exercises.spokenText: A Pedro le conocí en la universidad.
options: A Pedro le conocí en la universidad.
A Pedro lo conocí en la universidad.
A Pedro le conocí a él en la universidad.
A Pedro la conocí en la universidad.
exercises.answer: A Pedro le conocí en la universidad.
exercises.explanation: Standard LatAm: 'A Pedro lo conocí'. Spain leísmo: 'A Pedro le conocí'.

exercises.prompt: Spain leísmo — 'I phoned my brother yesterday': '___ llamé ayer (a mi hermano)' (one word).
exercises.explanation: Leísmo de persona: 'le llamé' instead of standard 'lo llamé'.

exercises.prompt: I saw him yesterday at the office
exercises.answer: Le vi ayer en la oficina
exercises.explanation: Spain leísmo: 'Le vi'. Standard would be 'Lo vi'.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'Le compré (el libro)' considered non-standard leísmo, while 'Le vi (a Juan)' is RAE-accepted?
options: Because 'el libro' is non-human; leísmo de cosa isn't accepted
Because 'le' can only be plural here
Because the verb 'comprar' doesn't take leísmo
exercises.answer: Because 'el libro' is non-human; leísmo de cosa isn't accepted
exercises.explanation: RAE only accepts leísmo for masculine HUMAN direct objects. 'Leísmo de cosa' (book, chair, idea) stays non-standard.

exercises.prompt: Which is a CORRECT use of leísmo de persona?
options: Le invité a Juan a mi boda.
Le veo el coche desde aquí.
exercises.answer: Le invité a Juan a mi boda.
exercises.explanation: Only the first has a masculine human DO. The others use 'le' for things or animals — non-standard leísmo de cosa/animal.

lessons.title: Laísmo — 'la' as feminine indirect (non-standard)
lessons.description: Madrid's stigmatized variant — recognize but don't write

exercises.prompt: Which is the laísmo variant?
options: Yo la verdad dije a María.
exercises.explanation: Laísmo: 'la' replaces standard 'le' for feminine indirect object. Non-standard, common in Madrid speech.

exercises.prompt: Laísmo is:
exercises.explanation: RAE rejects laísmo. It's a Madrid/central Spain spoken feature. In writing it marks the text as casual Madrid speech or as ungrammatical.

exercises.prompt: Convert laísmo 'La regalé un perfume a mi madre' to standard: '___ regalé un perfume a mi madre' (one word).
exercises.explanation: Standard system: 'le' is gender-neutral for IO. The 'la' in laísmo is the Madrid feminine marking.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'La compré un vestido a mi hija' laísmo?
options: Because 'mi hija' is the indirect object and feminine 'la' is Madrid-marking
exercises.answer: Because 'mi hija' is the indirect object and feminine 'la' is Madrid-marking
exercises.explanation: The IO is 'a mi hija' — standard would be 'le compré un vestido'. Laísmo marks the IO feminine: 'la compré un vestido'.

exercises.prompt: Match laísmo to standard
exercises.explanation: Each Madrid laísmo 'la/las' for feminine IO becomes standard 'le/les'.

A esa niña le dije que se callara y no me hizo caso.
A esa niña lo dije que se callara y no me hizo caso.
A esa niña les dije que se callara y no me hizo caso.
exercises.answer: A esa niña la dije que se callara y no me hizo caso.
exercises.explanation: Standard would be 'le dije'. The 'la dije' is classic Madrid laísmo.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite to standard: 'Las conté el secreto a mis amigas.' → '___ conté el secreto a mis amigas' (one word).
exercises.explanation: Standard plural IO is 'les' regardless of gender. Laísmo plural is 'las' for feminine.

exercises.prompt: True or false: laísmo is the feminine mirror of leísmo (i.e., applies to direct objects).
options: False — laísmo applies to indirect objects
True — both apply to direct objects
exercises.answer: False — laísmo applies to indirect objects
exercises.explanation: Leísmo = 'le' for masculine human DO (where standard says 'lo'). Laísmo = 'la' for feminine IO (where standard says 'le'). They operate on different objects.

exercises.prompt: I told her the news yesterday
exercises.explanation: Laísmo: 'la conté' (instead of standard 'le conté'). 'A ella' is IO of 'contar'.

exercises.prompt: You're writing a formal business email to a female client. Which is correct?
options: Le envío adjunta la propuesta para su revisión.
La envío adjunta la propuesta para su revisión.
Lo envío adjunta la propuesta para su revisión.
Les envío adjunta la propuesta para su revisión.
exercises.answer: Le envío adjunta la propuesta para su revisión.
exercises.explanation: In formal writing always use the standard 'le' for IO regardless of the recipient's gender. Laísmo 'la envío' would mark the email as casual Madrid speech.

lessons.title: Loísmo — recognition only
lessons.description: The stigmatized mirror of laísmo: 'lo' for masculine IO

exercises.prompt: What does loísmo do?
options: Replaces 'le' with 'lo' for masculine indirect objects
Replaces 'la' with 'lo' for feminine direct objects
Replaces 'le' with 'la' for feminine indirect objects
Replaces 'lo' with 'le' for masculine direct objects
exercises.answer: Replaces 'le' with 'lo' for masculine indirect objects
exercises.explanation: Loísmo: 'lo dije la verdad a Juan' instead of standard 'le dije la verdad'. Rare, stigmatized.

exercises.prompt: Loísmo is:
options: strongly stigmatized; rare even in casual speech
exercises.answer: strongly stigmatized; rare even in casual speech
exercises.explanation: Loísmo carries social stigma. You'll meet it in some rural speech and in older literature. Never produce it in your own Spanish.

exercises.prompt: Convert loísmo 'Lo dije a Juan que viniera' to standard: '___ dije a Juan que viniera' (one word).
exercises.explanation: Standard: 'le' for masculine (and feminine) IO. Loísmo 'lo' for IO is stigmatized.

exercises.prompt: Which is loísmo?
options: Lo pegué un grito a mi hermano.
La di un beso a mi madre.
exercises.answer: Lo pegué un grito a mi hermano.
exercises.explanation: 'A mi hermano' is the IO of 'pegar un grito'. Loísmo: 'lo pegué un grito'. Standard: 'le pegué un grito'.

Le dije la verdad a Juan.

exercises.explanation: Loísmo and laísmo apply to IO; leísmo to DO. The standard system uses 'le' for any IO.

exercises.prompt: Why is loísmo more stigmatized than laísmo even though they're structurally parallel?
options: Historical and sociolinguistic accident — laísmo became a Madrid prestige feature; loísmo never did
Loísmo only appears in non-native speech
Loísmo is technically the same as leísmo
exercises.answer: Historical and sociolinguistic accident — laísmo became a Madrid prestige feature; loísmo never did
exercises.explanation: Both are non-standard, but laísmo entrenched itself in Madrid speech across classes; loísmo stayed associated with rural/non-prestige speech and got stigmatized.

exercises.prompt: Spot the loísmo
exercises.spokenText: A mi padre lo regalé una corbata por su cumpleaños.
exercises.explanation: Standard: 'A mi padre le regalé una corbata'. The 'lo' for IO is loísmo.

exercises.prompt: 'Los compré flores (a los chicos)' → standard version
exercises.explanation: Standard plural IO is 'les'. The 'los compré' for IO is plural loísmo.

exercises.prompt: Should you produce loísmo in your own Spanish writing?
exercises.explanation: Loísmo is stigmatized and non-standard. Recognize it when you read older or rural texts; never write it yourself.

exercises.prompt: True or false: 'Lo dije a Juan' (meaning 'I told it to Juan') is loísmo.
options: False — here 'lo' is the DO (it = the thing said); not loísmo
True — if Juan is the subject
exercises.answer: False — here 'lo' is the DO (it = the thing said); not loísmo
exercises.explanation: 'Decir algo a alguien': 'lo' is the DO ('it = the thing'), 'a Juan' is the IO. 'Lo dije a Juan' = 'I said it to Juan' — standard. Loísmo only arises if 'lo' replaces the IO.

lessons.description: Spot the variant and convert to standard, and vice versa

exercises.prompt: What is 'le' in: 'A Carlos le conocí en Madrid'?

exercises.answer: leísmo de persona — DO that should be 'lo'
exercises.explanation: 'Conocer a Carlos' = DO. Standard 'lo conocí'. Spain 'le conocí' = accepted leísmo.

exercises.explanation: 'Contar algo a Marta' = IO. Standard 'le conté'. Madrid laísmo 'la conté' — non-standard.

exercises.prompt: What is 'lo' in: 'A Juan lo regalé un libro'?

exercises.explanation: Spain leísmo for masculine human DO: 'le conocí'.

exercises.spokenText: Le vi a Pablo ayer y la dije a Ana lo que me contaste.
options: Le vi a Pablo ayer y la dije a Ana lo que me contaste.

Le vi a Pablo ayer y le dije a Ana lo que me contaste.
Lo vi a Pablo ayer y la dije a Ana lo que me contaste.
exercises.answer: Le vi a Pablo ayer y la dije a Ana lo que me contaste.

exercises.prompt: 'A Ana la pregunté la hora' — standard version
exercises.answer: A Ana le pregunté la hora
exercises.explanation: 'Preguntar la hora a Ana' = IO. Standard: 'le pregunté'.

exercises.prompt: You're translating a Madrid novel into formal Spanish for a Latin American audience. The text says 'Le invité a Juan y la dije a María que viniera'. The cleanest standard rewrite is:
options: Lo invité a Juan y le dije a María que viniera.
Le invité a Juan y le dije a María que viniera.
Lo invité a Juan y la dije a María que viniera.
Les invité a los dos y les dije que vinieran.

exercises.explanation: 'Invitar a Juan' = DO masc. → 'lo invité' (strip leísmo). 'Decir a María que viniera' = IO → 'le dije' (strip laísmo).

exercises.prompt: Which sentence would sound MOST natural in Bogotá, Colombia?

Le vi a Juan en la fiesta y la di tu mensaje.
Le vi a Juan en la fiesta y le di tu mensaje.
La vi a Juan en la fiesta y le di tu mensaje.
exercises.answer: Lo vi a Juan en la fiesta y le di tu mensaje.

topics.title: Discourse particles at C1 — vaya, hombre, anda, che
topics.description: Tiny words with big tonal payloads

guide.intro: By A2 you've met 'pues', 'bueno', 'vale', 'oye', 'mira'. At C1 you need the harder tier: 'vaya' (wow / what a...), 'hombre/mujer' (come on / softener), 'anda' (go on / really?), 'venga' (come on / OK), 'órale' (Mexican affirmation), 'che' (Argentine vocative), 'tío/tía' (Spain casual address). These particles don't translate cleanly — they carry tone, register, region, and stance. A learner who can sprinkle them correctly sounds native; one who misses them sounds robotic.

sections.text: Vaya — surprise, dismay, or sarcasm

'Vaya' literally means 'let it go' (subjunctive of 'ir'), but as a particle it functions like English 'wow' / 'sheesh' / 'what a...'. Front-loaded on a noun: 'vaya día' ('what a day'), 'vaya cara' ('what nerve'), 'vaya casa' ('what a house'). Alone as an exclamation: '¡Vaya!' ('wow' or 'oh dear'). Tone is everything — same word can be admiration, dismay, or sarcasm.

rows.source: ¡Vaya día! No he parado un segundo.
rows.translation: What a day! I haven't stopped for a second.

rows.source: Vaya, vaya. ¿Quién lo iba a decir?
rows.translation: Well, well. Who would have thought?

rows.source: ¡Vaya cara tienes! Me has cogido el coche sin pedirlo.
rows.translation: What nerve! You took my car without asking.

sections.text: Hombre / mujer — 'come on' softener

Used as a particle, not literally. 'Hombre' said to anyone (regardless of their gender) softens or pushes back: 'Hombre, no exageres' ('Come on, don't exaggerate'). 'Mujer' (less common) is sometimes used with women specifically. Position: usually opening, occasionally medial. Tone is mild — a friendly nudge, not aggression.

rows.source: Hombre, claro que te ayudo. Para eso somos amigos.
rows.translation: Of course I'll help. That's what friends are for.

rows.source: Hombre, tampoco te pases.
rows.translation: Come on, don't go too far.

rows.source: Hombre, ¿qué quieres que te diga?
rows.translation: Look, what do you want me to say?

sections.text: Anda — surprise, mock disbelief

Literally 'walk', but as a particle: 'really?', 'go on', 'oh come on'. '¡Anda ya!' is the strongest form — 'no way, get out of here'. Used for genuine surprise, mock skepticism, or playful dismissal. Heavily Spain — Latin Americans use it but less.

rows.source: —Me ha tocado la lotería. —¡Anda ya, no me lo creo!
rows.translation: I won the lottery. — No way, I don't believe you!

rows.source: ¡Anda! No sabía que vivieras aquí.
rows.translation: Oh wow! I didn't know you lived here.

rows.source: Anda, dame un poco más de tiempo.
rows.translation: Go on, give me a bit more time.

sections.text: Venga (Spain) — let's go / come on / OK

Spain everywhere. 'Venga' (subjunctive of 'venir') means 'come on', 'let's go', 'OK then'. At the end of a phone call: '¡Venga, hasta luego!' = 'OK, bye!'. Urging: 'venga, vamos' = 'come on, let's go'. Mild disbelief: 'venga ya' = 'come on, really?'.
Órale (Mexico) — affirmation / surprise

Mexican universal particle. 'Órale' = 'OK', 'right on', 'wow', or 'let's go'. '¡Órale, qué padre!' = 'Wow, how cool!'. '¡Órale, vámonos!' = 'OK, let's go!'. Almost untranslatable — Mexico's answer to 'venga'.
Regional vocatives — che, tío/tía, mano

'Che' opens or punctuates phrases in Argentina/Uruguay — 'che, ¿qué hacés?' ('hey, what are you doing?'). 'Tío/tía' (Spain casual) addresses a friend: 'tío, mira esto' ('dude, look at this'). 'Mano' (Mexico, Central America) = 'bro' (from 'hermano'). 'Wey/güey' (Mexico) similar. 'Pana' (Caribbean, Venezuela) = 'buddy'.
Vulgar register — joder, coño (Spain)

Spain's everyday interjections include 'joder' (literally an f-word, but as interjection more like English 'damn') and 'coño' (vulgar in Latin America, mildly so in Spain). Used for emphasis, frustration, surprise. RECOGNIZE these so you don't miss the speaker's tone — but be careful producing them, especially with strangers, in Latin America (where they're rougher), or in any formal context.

Particles stack in real speech: 'Hombre, pues, anda, mira...' Each adds a layer of tone. Don't try to drop them all at once — pick one or two per utterance and you'll sound native rather than performative.

exercises.explanation: 'Venga' as urging particle + 'vamos' = 'come on, let's go'.

exercises.prompt: At the end of a Spanish phone call: 'Venga, hasta luego'. What is 'venga'?
exercises.explanation: 'Venga' tags the end of phone calls in Spain — 'OK, bye'. Native marker.

exercises.prompt: What's the Mexican equivalent of Spain's 'venga' in '¡Venga, qué padre!'?
exercises.explanation: 'Órale' is the Mexican universal — affirmation, urging, surprise. '¡Órale, qué padre!' = 'wow, how cool!'.

exercises.prompt: Fill the Mexican particle: '___, vámonos al cine.' (one word for the urging 'OK / let's')
exercises.explanation: 'Órale' urges or affirms. Common Mexican opener.

exercises.prompt: Match particle to region
exercises.explanation: All four function as casual affirmation / urging particles, but each is regionally marked.

exercises.prompt: Which country?
exercises.spokenText: Órale, güey, ¿qué onda?
exercises.explanation: Two strong Mexican markers: 'órale' + 'güey' (or 'wey') + '¿qué onda?'.

exercises.prompt: Which country?
exercises.spokenText: Venga, tío, no me digas eso.
exercises.explanation: 'Venga' + vocative 'tío' = Spain casual speech.

exercises.prompt: 'Come on, let's go to the movies'
exercises.explanation: Spain urging: 'venga, vamos'. Mexico would be 'órale, vámonos'. Argentina 'dale, vamos'.

exercises.prompt: Spain phone closure — 'OK then, bye': '___, hasta luego' (one word).
exercises.explanation: Phone-close 'venga' is so common in Spain that learners who skip it sound stiff.

exercises.prompt: In Mexico, you say '¡Órale!' as someone tells you they got a promotion. What are you expressing?
exercises.explanation: '¡Órale!' as standalone reaction = enthusiastic approval, surprise — 'wow!'.

lessons.title: Regional vocatives — che, tío/tía, mano, wey
lessons.description: How to call out a friend without sounding regional in the wrong place

exercises.prompt: 'Che, ¿vos venís?' — which country?
exercises.explanation: 'Che' as a vocative + voseo 'vos venís' = Río de la Plata.

exercises.prompt: 'Tío, mira esto.' — which country?
exercises.explanation: 'Tío/tía' as casual address ('dude/man') is Spain. Latin America keeps 'tío' for literal uncle.

exercises.prompt: 'Wey, ¿qué onda?' — which country?
exercises.explanation: 'Wey' (or 'güey') + '¿qué onda?' = Mexico. Like English 'dude, what's up?'.

exercises.prompt: Fill the Argentine vocative: '___, ¿vos sabés a qué hora llega?' (one word, the classic Argentine opener)
exercises.explanation: 'Che' is the Argentine universal vocative. Goes in any position; works with strangers, friends, or family.

exercises.prompt: Match vocative to region
exercises.explanation: Each casual vocative is strongly regional.

exercises.prompt: Identify the region
exercises.spokenText: Mano, no manches, ¿en serio te pasó eso?
exercises.explanation: 'Mano' (from 'hermano') + 'no manches' = Mexican casual.

exercises.prompt: Which vocative is safe to use almost anywhere without sounding too regional?
exercises.explanation: 'Amigo' is regionally neutral. The others are strongly marked: 'tío' = Spain, 'che' = Arg, 'güey' = Mex.

exercises.prompt: Dude, did you see the game?
exercises.explanation: Spain casual address: 'tío'. Argentine would be 'Che, ¿viste el partido?'.

exercises.prompt: Mexican casual — fill the vocative: '___, vamos al taquería.' (one-word opener, the Mexican 'bro')
exercises.explanation: 'Mano' (short for 'hermano') is a friendly Mexican vocative. 'Wey/güey' is rougher.

exercises.prompt: Mixing 'che' and 'tío' in the same conversation is:
options: a dialect mismatch — picks two countries at once
exercises.answer: a dialect mismatch — picks two countries at once
exercises.explanation: 'Che' belongs to Argentina/Uruguay; 'tío' belongs to Spain. Stacking them marks you as a confused learner.

lessons.title: Vulgar register — joder, coño
lessons.description: Recognize Spain's everyday interjections without producing them carelessly

exercises.prompt: In Spain, 'joder' as an interjection (not a verb) is most like English:
exercises.explanation: '¡Joder!' as interjection = English 'damn' or 'shit'. The verb meaning is much stronger; the interjection is widespread casual.

exercises.prompt: In Latin America, 'coño' is generally:
options: stronger / more vulgar than in Spain
exercises.answer: stronger / more vulgar than in Spain
exercises.explanation: 'Coño' refers to female genitalia. In Spain it's a mild interjection ('coño, qué frío'). In Latin America it's much rougher.

exercises.prompt: Should you produce 'joder' in a job interview in Spain?
options: No — vulgar register only with friends
exercises.answer: No — vulgar register only with friends
exercises.explanation: Even in Spain, 'joder' is casual / vulgar register. Reserve it for friends. Never in formal contexts.

exercises.prompt: Recognize: '¡Joder, qué frío hace!' — translate the interjection only (one English word).
exercises.explanation: Spain casual: 'joder' as interjection is roughly 'damn' / 'shit'. The sentence: 'Damn, it's so cold!'

exercises.prompt: Which is the SAFEST clean substitute for 'joder' as an interjection?
exercises.explanation: 'Jolín' and 'jope' are euphemistic versions of 'joder' — totally clean and used by everyone in Spain.

exercises.prompt: Pick the speaker's emotion
exercises.spokenText: Coño, qué calor está haciendo hoy.
exercises.explanation: Spain casual 'coño' as opener + 'qué calor' = venting about the heat.

exercises.prompt: Match interjection to register
exercises.explanation: Same emotion, very different registers. Pick by audience.

exercises.prompt: True or false: producing 'joder' in front of a Latin American audience is the same as in Spain.
options: False — much more shocking in LatAm
exercises.answer: False — much more shocking in LatAm
exercises.explanation: Spain has normalized 'joder' as casual emphasis. Latin America generally hears it as the original obscenity.

exercises.prompt: Clean rewrite — replace the vulgar interjection: '___, qué frío.' (one word, polite version)
exercises.explanation: Clean alternatives: 'vaya', 'jolín', 'madre mía'. 'Vaya' is the most universal.

exercises.prompt: What's the right move when you hear vulgar particles from a native speaker?
options: Recognize the tone, don't necessarily reproduce them
exercises.answer: Recognize the tone, don't necessarily reproduce them
exercises.explanation: C1 listening: understand the emotional load. C1 speaking: pick your register. Copying every vulgar particle back can sound forced or accidentally offensive.

lessons.title: Stacking particles in real speech
lessons.description: Pulling apart 'hombre, pues mira, anda, vamos a ver'

exercises.prompt: In 'Hombre, pues mira, no sé qué decirte', what does 'hombre' contribute?
exercises.explanation: 'Hombre' opens the response gently — like English 'well, look...'.

exercises.prompt: In the same sentence, what does 'pues' contribute?
exercises.explanation: 'Pues' is the all-purpose discourse opener: 'well / so'.

exercises.prompt: And 'mira'?
exercises.explanation: 'Mira' as discourse particle = 'look' / 'listen' — calls attention to what follows.

exercises.prompt: Match particle to its tonal role
exercises.explanation: Stacked particles each pull a different lever — softening, opening, calling attention, expressing surprise.

exercises.prompt: Identify the stack
exercises.spokenText: Anda, hombre, pues mira lo que ha pasado.
exercises.explanation: Four particles in one phrase, each adding a tone: 'anda' (surprise), 'hombre' (softener), 'pues' (opener), 'mira' (attention).

exercises.prompt: Add a softener to: '___, no exageres.' (one word, 'come on')
exercises.explanation: 'Hombre' softens the pushback. 'Mujer' works with women specifically.

exercises.prompt: Add an opener to: '___, no sé qué decirte.' (one word, 'well / so')
exercises.explanation: 'Pues' is the universal discourse opener. 'Bueno' works similarly.

exercises.prompt: 'Come on, listen, I don't know what to tell you'
exercises.answer: Hombre , mira , no sé qué decirte
exercises.explanation: Stacking 'hombre' (softener) + 'mira' (attention) + the actual content.

exercises.prompt: A learner who never uses any particles in conversation sounds:
exercises.explanation: Particles ARE the texture of native speech. Skipping them all makes you sound like a textbook reader, even if every sentence is grammatical.

exercises.prompt: A learner who stacks four particles in every sentence sounds:
exercises.explanation: Over-stacking is its own tell. Native speakers use one or two particles per utterance — adding four every time is performative.

topics.title: C1 mixed review
topics.description: Pull it all together — register, idioms, grammar, regional

guide.intro: By the end of C1, you should be able to switch between formal and informal Spanish at will, recognize whichever regional dialect you encounter, drop the right refrán at the right moment, and write in any register from board memo to op-ed. This review lesson stitches all eight strands together: business formality, academic hedging, society vocabulary, idioms, advanced grammar, debate moves, regional differences, and news register.

sections.text: Register dial — formal ↔ neutral ↔ casual

C1 is fundamentally about the register dial. Same idea, three registers: formal 'Le agradeceríamos su respuesta'; neutral 'Esperamos su respuesta'; casual 'Espero que me contestes pronto'. Native speakers move between these all day; you should too.

rows.source: Formal: Le rogamos que confirme su asistencia.
rows.translation: We kindly ask you to confirm your attendance.

rows.source: Neutral: Por favor confirma si vienes.
rows.translation: Please confirm if you're coming.

rows.source: Casual: Avísame si te apuntas.
rows.translation: Let me know if you're in.

sections.text: Refrán + grammar combo

The C1 power move: combine a refrán with advanced grammar. 'Si hubiera prestado más atención al refrán, no habría caído en la trampa' ('if I had heeded the proverb, I wouldn't have fallen into the trap'). Stack past unreal subjunctive on top of folk wisdom for full effect.

rows: No todo lo que reluce es oro

sections.text: If you can hold a 15-minute formal meeting, switch to chatting with a friend over coffee, and then read El País or Clarín in the evening without effort, you've made it to C1.

La autora cuyo obra leí ganó el premio
La autora cuyos obra leí ganó el premio
La autora cuya obras leí ganó el premio
exercises.answer: La autora cuya obra leí ganó el premio
exercises.explanation: 'Cuya' agrees with 'obra' (fem. sg., the following noun), not with 'autora'.
